sources.source: Monitoring and Alerting on SLOs (Google SRE Workbook, Chapter 5)

items.item: burn rate measures how fast, relative to the SLO, a service consumes its error budget
multiple burn rates and time windows catch both a fast, sharp failure and a slower but still significant one
the recommended thresholds: 2% budget in one hour and 5% in six hours page, 10% in three days tickets

sources.source: This topic's own real thirty-day pipeline run (SQLite, in-process)

items.item: finish-time freshness measured a perfect month while the consumer's own read point was stale for six real days
the six-day outage alone consumed many times a tier-one monthly error budget, and the SRE Workbook's own ticket-alert rule fired exactly during it

The hook's dashboard is not a strawman of bad monitoring -- a pipeline SLA genuinely is useful information, just a different one than freshness-at-read. The point isn't that finish-time monitoring is worthless, it's that it answers a narrower question than the one a consumer-facing SLO needs answered.

A reader might assume 'consumer's read point' means instrumenting every dashboard and API individually, which doesn't scale. In practice, teams approximate it by measuring the final materialized artifact's own last-successful-refresh timestamp -- close enough to the true read point as long as nothing caches that artifact further downstream, a caveat worth naming rather than leaving implicit.

Tiering isn't just 'customer-facing gets a tighter number' -- the SRE Workbook's own framing ties the tier to what an error budget policy actually commits an organization to doing once it's exhausted; a tier with no real policy behind it is just a label, not a working SLO.

at.step: Reveal: SLO targets per tier, and the error budget

items.item: The error budget's arithmetic depends entirely on the measurement window chosen (a day, a week, a rolling thirty days) -- the same SLO percentage buys a very different number of allowed-late hours depending on the window, which is why this topic states the window explicitly rather than leaving 'the SLO' as a bare percentage.

The SRE Workbook's multi-burn-rate table is itself a tradeoff, not a universal constant -- its own text names the alternative (a single fixed window) as trading precision against recall; the specific percentages (2%, 5%, 10%) are the Workbook's own recommended starting point for a request-based SLI, adapted here to a once-a-day freshness check's natural granularity rather than applied unchanged.

A reader carrying forward topic 3's backfill vocabulary might assume 'spending the budget on purpose' means a backfill is free as long as budget remains -- it still costs real budget, the difference is only that the cost was anticipated and approved beforehand rather than discovered after the fact in an incident review.

The real lab's finish-time SLI staying at a perfect score the entire month isn't a contrived result to make the point land -- it is the realistic failure mode this topic exists to warn about: a pipeline-level SLA can be contractually met in full while a consumer-facing promise is broken, with no contradiction in the data at all.

This topic deliberately reuses the shop's own `fct_orders` table (seen already in the course) rather than introducing a new example, so the freshness-at-read-point distinction lands on a table the learner already has a mental model of, instead of competing for attention with a new domain.

The topic's own thirty-day window and the SRE Workbook's own thirty-day example window are the same length by deliberate choice, not coincidence -- it lets the Workbook's percentage-based thresholds (2%, 5%, 10% of budget) carry over to this topic's own numbers without rescaling, which the Internals deep dive calls out explicitly rather than leaving it to be noticed.

A reader might read 'tier' as a property of a table fixed forever at creation time; in practice a table's tier can change as its consumers change (an internal exploration table that later gets wired into a customer-facing product needs its SLO re-set, not inherited from its old tier).
